source.title: Concrete examples of the rate of convergence of Chernoff approximations: numerical results for the heat semigroup and open questions on them (with appendix: full list of pictures and Python code)

accepted.question_text: Let UC_b(R) be the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real functions with the sup norm, and let Lf=f'' generate the heat semigroup e^{tL}. Existing rate theorems for Chernoff approximations require smoothness and domain conditions, such as membership in powers of D(L). If those conditions fail, for example when an initial condition f is differentiable only once but not twice and f' is Hölder continuous with exponent 1/2, what is the asymptotic convergence rate of C(t/n)^n f to e^{tL}f as n tends to infinity? More generally, how does the rate depend on the smoothness of f and on whether the Chernoff function C has first-order or higher-order Chernoff tangency to L when f is not in the regularity class covered by the known theorem?
accepted.context_brief: Chernoff rates below known regularity hypotheses

Also we see from theorem 4 that Chernoff functions with higher order of Chernoff tangency toLprovide a better rate of convergence.

The main question attacked in the paper.What happens if conditions of the above theorem 4 do not hold? For example, what the convergence rate will be iffis differentiable only once but not twice, andf ′ is e.g. H¨ older continuous with H¨ older exponent equal to 1/2? Then f /∈D(∂ 2) and the above theorem say nothing about the rate of convergence.

For initial conditions that are good enough andtfixed, Chernoff function with Chernoff tangency of orderk(by conjecture from [17] and by theorem 4 above) should provide∥u(t,·)−u n(t,·)∥=O(1/n k) as n→ ∞. However, iff̸∈Dthen nothing is known on the rate of convergence.

accepted.question_text: Let UC_b(R,R) be the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on R with the sup norm. Given arbitrary a,b,c in UC_b(R,R) with a(x) bounded below by a positive constant, let L be the second-order variable-coefficient differential operator (Lf)(x)=a(x)f''(x)+b(x)f'(x)+c(x)f(x) on C_b^∞(R,R), whose closure generates a C_0-semigroup e^{tL}. Does there exist an explicitly computable family C(t) of bounded linear operators on UC_b(R,R), expressed directly in terms of a,b,c,f,x and not using e^{tL} even implicitly, such that C is a Chernoff function for L and, on some dense subspace D, the approximation error satisfies ||e^{tL}f-C(t/n)^n f|| ≤ M/q^n for constants M>0 and q>1 for all sufficiently large n? If such superfast Chernoff approximations do not exist, what obstruction proves their impossibility?

evidence.quote: In the List of open problems in the One-parameter semigroups theory [13] there is the following problem:Provide a concrete example of a super-fast (at least exponentially) converging Chernoff approximation to a semigroup generated by a first-order differential operator with variable coefficients, with Chernoff function explicitly expressed in terms of these coefficients and without circulus vitiosus of any kind, e.g. in the form of using the values of the semigroup for creating a Chernoff function for it.
The open problemis to find a family (C(t))t≥0 of linear bounded operators defined everywhere inU C b(R,R) which has the following three properties:
There exists a dense linear subspaceDinU C b(R,R) and constantsM >0, q >1, n 0 >0 such that ∥etLf−C(t/n) nf∥ ≤M/q n for alln≥n 0 and allf∈D;

Cis defined by an explicitly given formula (C(t)f)(x) =F(a, b, c, f, x) and the calculation ofe tL is not included into this formula, even in a hidden way, so expression etL = lim n→∞ C(t/n) n is free from circulus vitiosus of any kind and can be used as a practical method of calculation ofe tL.

Effective methods for constructing superfast converging Chernoff approximations for this operatorLare not known at present. However, there are no fundamental objections to their existence either, which presents a challenge to either find such approximations or to prove that they are impossible for some reason.

accepted.question_text: For the heat equation u_t(t,x)=u_xx(t,x) on the real line, work in the Banach space UC_b(R) of bounded uniformly continuous real functions with the sup norm. Let Lf=f'' generate the heat semigroup e^{tL}. For t=1/2, compare the exact solution e^{tL}u0 with Chernoff products G(t/n)^n u0 and S(t/n)^n u0, where G is first-order Chernoff tangent to L and S is second-order Chernoff tangent to L. Write d_n^G=||e^{tL}u0-G(t/n)^n u0|| and d_n^S=||e^{tL}u0-S(t/n)^n u0||, and estimate log d_n approximately as alpha log n plus beta, where alpha is the order of decreasing error and beta is the free term. Why does the log-log relationship between the approximation error and n have very different quality of linear fit for different initial conditions? In particular, what theoretical mechanism makes the fit essentially perfect for u0(x)=sin x and u0(x)=cos x and also good for the nonsmooth initial condition u0(x)=|sin x|^(1/4), while the smooth initial condition u0(x)=exp(-x^4) gives a noticeably poorer fit, contrary to a naive expectation that higher smoothness should improve the fit?
accepted.context_brief: Quality of log-log linear error fits

For eacht≥0 we introduce linear bounded operators G(t) andS(t) inFas (G(t)f)(x) = 1 2 f(x) + 1 4 f(x+ 2 √ t) + 1 4 f(x−2 √ t), (S(t)f)(x) = 2 3 f(x) + 1 6 f(x+ √ 6t) + 1 6 f(x− √ 6t).

Paul Chernoff’s theorem [3] implies that for eacht >0, eachu 0 ∈ Fsequences dG n =∥e tLu0 −G(t/n) nu0∥, d S n =∥e tLu0 −S(t/n) nu0∥ converge to 0 asn→ ∞, but it saysnothingabout the rate of convergence.
For all of them, we numerically calculated lnd G n ≈α G lnn+β G,lnd S n ≈α S lnn+β S. We callαthe order of decreasing error,βthe free term of decreasing error.
These are effects that we see numerically but do not know how to explain theoretically:

1. The linear approximation of error lnd n vs. lnnisnot equally perfect, and it is often different for different initial conditions. But foru 0(x) = sin(x),u 0(x) = cos(x) the error isidentical. For smoothu 0(x) = sin(x) we see that points fit the line perfectly (fig. 1.2), as well as for non-smoothu 0(x) =|sin(x)| 1/4, see fig. 3.2. But for smoothu 0(x) =e −x4 we see that points do not fit the line well (fig. 14.2). It seems that a higher smoothness provides a worse line fit, but foru 0(x) = sin(x) the fit is very good.
